summary: Analyzes security threats to Multipath TCP, which lets one connection use several paths, and what is needed to keep it as secure as regular TCP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipath TCP can use several address pairs for one connection, which creates new ways to redirect traffic or interfere with the connection. RFC 6181 analyzes those threats and recommends checks and protections for address changes.

questions: what are the security threats to multipath tcp
what is a flooding attack in mptcp
why do nats make mptcp security hard
subtitle: Threats introduced when one TCP connection can use multiple address pairs.

tldr.problem: Allowing a TCP connection to use multiple source-destination address pairs introduces flooding and hijacking risks beyond those of single-path TCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6181 analyzes attacks on a general multi-address MPTCP design, including off-path and time-shifted attackers, and recommends reachability checks, keyed integrity protection, and replay protection.
tldr.outcome: The Informational analysis was written as input for MPTCP designers. It seeks to keep MPTCP no less secure than current TCP, rather than to make it more secure.

today: RFC 6181 is Informational and the supplied metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Scope of the Threat Analysis
sections.content:
The analysis covers a version of Multipath TCP in which endpoints have multiple IP addresses and different source-destination address pairs represent different paths. It focuses on vulnerabilities added by this capability compared with single-path TCP.

Off-path attackers and attackers who are on the path briefly and later leave are in scope. Attackers continuously on the path are out of scope because the RFC treats their attacks as existing TCP threats. The goal is for MPTCP to be as secure as current TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: This document focuses on risks caused by adding multiple paths to one TCP connection. It does not analyze attacks that already apply to an attacker who remains on a regular TCP path.

sections.title: Assumed MPTCP Behavior
sections.content:
The RFC assumes that a connection begins with the TCP three-way handshake on one address pair and uses a single data sequence-number space. It treats the connection as identified by the four values: source address, source port, destination address, and destination port.

After setup, an endpoint can add addresses through explicit signaling or implicitly by using an address as the source of a packet. The RFC warns that ingress filtering is not widespread enough to serve as the basis for MPTCP security.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection starts like TCP and initially uses one address pair. Later, endpoints can signal additional addresses, so the other endpoint must decide whether to trust them.

sections.title: Flooding by Adding a Victim Address
sections.content:
An attacker can try to add a victim's address to an MPTCP connection, then cause the source to send traffic to that address while it believes it is sending to the attacker. A victim with no matching connection may send reset packets, but traffic already in flight can still cause harm.

The RFC describes a second flooding risk: an attacker can advertise many addresses, causing a peer to send traffic to many destinations if it opens subflows to all of them. A reachability check before using a new address can prevent these attacks; the check can include a nonce that the attacker cannot predict.
sections.plainLanguage: A malicious endpoint might ask a peer to send connection traffic to an unrelated address. Checking that the new address is reachable before sending data helps prevent this redirection.

sections.title: Hijacking, NATs and Recommendations
sections.content:
An attacker who learns the connection's address and port values may try to add its own address and inject or intercept data. A cookie exchanged in cleartext can stop an off-path attacker, but a time-shifted attacker can capture it while on the path and use it later. Keyed HMAC protection narrows exposure of the key, but NAT address rewriting complicates protecting the address itself.

The RFC recommends a reachability check using a random nonce before adding an address, a key exchange on the first subflow followed by keyed HMACs for later additions, support for a pre-shared key, and replay protection. It also recommends extensibility for stronger security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Address changes need protection against attackers who observe or alter connection messages. The RFC recommends confirming reachability, authenticating later changes, and preventing old messages from being replayed.
